The Indian sabertooth Evermannella melanoderma is a mesopelagic aulopiform fish whose life-history strategy reflects the low-productivity environment of the deep scattering layer. Field surveys of adult specimens collected in the tropical Indian Ocean indicate that the maximum recorded total length for this species reaches 12.7 cm [Li = 12.7 cm], a modest size consistent with its position as a mid-trophic-level predator. Sexual maturation, as determined through histological examination of gonadal tissue, occurs when individuals attain a standard length of 6 cm [Lp = 6 cm], marking the transition to the reproductively active phase. At this developmental milestone, the corresponding wet weight measured in freshly caught individuals averages 1.1 grams [Wwp = 1.1 grams], reflecting the allometric relationship between length and mass in this slender-bodied taxa. These morphological benchmarks provide a useful framework for understanding the timing of reproductive investment in a species adapted to the relatively stable but food-limited conditions of the mesopelagic zone, where growth appears to be slow, and energy is preferentially directed toward body tissue upkeep over rapid development.

Reproductive output in Evermannella melanoderma has been characterized through controlled laboratory observations of gravid females maintained at a stable temperature of 8 °C [T = 8 °C]. Under these thermal conditions, each spawning event yields roughly 104 eggs [N_R_i = each spawning event yields roughly 104 eggs], with individual females producing approximately one clutch per year [F_R_i = approximately one clutch per year]. This low annual fecundity is typical of mesopelagic taxa that produce relatively large, yolk-rich oocytes. The reliance on infrequent spawning events suggests that E. melanoderma invests considerable energy per offspring, a strategy that may enhance larval survival in the oligotrophic waters where this species primarily resides.

Egg diameter measurements taken from freshly spawned oocytes of the Indian sabertooth provide insight into the substantial maternal investment per offspring. The average egg size is approximately 0.9 millimeters in diameter, which corresponds to a mean wet weight at birth of 0.00038 grams [Wwb = 0.00038 grams] based on the spherical volume calculation for a translucent, pelagic egg. This value indicates that each egg represents a significant fraction of maternal body reserves, consistent with the production of relatively large, well-provisioned propagules that are characteristic of species inhabiting environments where food availability for larvae is unpredictable. The egg size is comparable to that reported for other deep-sea aulopiforms and suggests a lecithotrophic larval phase during which endogenous yolk reserves sustain the embryo through early development, a critical adaptation for survival in the nutrient-poor waters of the mesopelagic realm where exogenous prey items are scarce for newly hatched individuals.

The growth trajectory from the larval stage to the attainment of maximum adult dimensions in Evermannella melanoderma follows a predictable allometric pattern. Based on the length-weight relationship derived from a large series of wild-caught specimens spanning the full size range, the asymptotic wet weight corresponding to the ultimate total length of 12.7 cm [Li = 12.7 cm] has been calculated as 11.9 grams [Wwi = 11.9 grams]. This value, which represents the maximum body mass an individual can achieve under optimal feeding conditions, is generated from a power-law function in which weight scales disproportionately with length, reflecting the species' fusiform body shape and relatively low condition factor. Young-of-the-year juveniles collected during midwater trawls exhibit a rapid increase in mass during the first few months of exogenous feeding, though growth decelerates considerably as individuals approach their maximum size. The ultimate body mass of roughly 12 grams is modest compared to epipelagic predators but is typical of mesopelagic fishes that maintain low metabolic rates and efficient energy use in their cold, dimly lit habitat.

Longevity estimates for the Indian sabertooth, derived from the analysis of daily growth increments in sagittal otoliths from a population sampled in the central Indian Ocean, indicate a maximum lifespan of approximately 3 years [am = approximately 3 years] at the typical ambient temperature of 8 °C, a value that aligns with the relatively fast-paced life history of small mesopelagic fishes at a temperature of 8 °C [T = 8 °C]. When maintained under controlled laboratory conditions at a constant 8 °C [T = 8 °C], the oldest observed individuals survived for 1,095 days [am = 1,095 days], confirming the otolith-based field estimate. This relatively brief lifespan, combined with the late age at first reproduction and low annual fecundity, positions E. melanoderma as an iteroparous species with a single, concentrated reproductive window before senescence. The species' natural mortality is likely elevated during the pelagic larval stage due to predation, but once individuals reach the juvenile phase and migrate to deeper waters, survivorship increases markedly, enabling most sexually mature adults to complete at least one full spawning season before age-related physiological decline sets in.
